item.title: 50 Cent’s “Street Fighter” Tops Box Office With $31 Million Debut
item.dc:creator: AllHipHop Staff
item.description: 50 Cent brought Balrog to the big screen as “Street Fighter” pulled in an estimated $51 million worldwide in its first weekend.
item.content:encoded:
50 Cent landed at the top of the box office with “Street Fighter,” which opened to an estimated $31 million in the United States and Canada.

The Paramount release took first place across 3,575 theaters, according to Sunday studio estimates reported by The Associated Press. International ticket sales added about $20 million, bringing its worldwide opening to roughly $51 million.

Box-office tracker The Numbers listed $13 million for Friday and $10.8 million for Saturday, with Sunday estimated at $7.2 million. AP said men made up 69% of the audience.

The film arrived in U.S. theaters on October 16 with 50 playing Balrog, the boxer from Capcom’s fighting games. Director Kitao Sakurai’s take put the characters in 1993, with Ryu and Ken drawn back into combat after Chun-Li recruited them for the World Warrior Tournament.

Andrew Koji played Ryu, Noah Centineo played Ken and Callina Liang played Chun-Li. The cast also included Eric André as Don Sauvage and Jason Momoa as Blanka, putting 50 in an ensemble built around the game’s fighters.

50 knew boxing years before he took the role, having practiced it from childhood through his teens. Balrog brought him back to the sport with an Australian coach. In the pre-release interviews, he also described the recovery side of the job, including massage and cryotherapy, alongside the pressure to match the character’s build.

The film reportedly cost $82 million to produce, excluding marketing and promotion. Capcom and Legendary jointly financed the adaptation as the game company pushed to bring its characters to audiences beyond gaming.

The first-place finish came with a B-minus CinemaScore, TheWrap reported, matching the grade for the 1994 “Street Fighter.” Its domestic start fell below the $38.5 million debut of “Mortal Kombat II,” another fighting-game adaptation released in May.

The weekend’s runner-up, “You Can See Everything,” brought in an estimated $15 million from 855 screens, according to AP, giving the Elizabeth Holmes documentary second place.

The new film nevertheless cleared the earlier “Street Fighter” movies’ opening weekends in unadjusted dollars. The Numbers recorded a $9.5 million debut for the 1994 film, while “Street Fighter: The Legend of Chun-Li” opened to $4.7 million in 2009.

Final domestic figures were due Monday.

item.title: Kelly Rowland & Tina Knowles Lead birthFUND Team At Houston Walk
item.dc:creator: AllHipHop Staff
item.description: Kelly Rowland and Tina Knowles will lead birthFUND’s Houston team, raising support for families seeking help with birth care.
item.content:encoded:
Kelly Rowland and Tina Knowles are heading back to Houston to lead birthFUND’s team at the first Third Ward Mile, putting their hometown ties behind a maternal-care fundraiser.

The two will serve as team captains alongside birthFUND founder Elaine Welteroth at the November 28 event, People reported. Both already support the nonprofit as family funders. The new role brings them to a community walk in the neighborhood where Knowles ran Headliners, the hair salon tied to Destiny’s Child’s beginnings.

“Every mother deserves to feel safe, supported and seen when she brings life into the world,” Rowland told People. Knowles added, “Third Ward helped me raise my girls.”

birthFUND’s program helps families pay for birth care. Its need-based grants cover perinatal care and midwifery support. Birth Center Equity vets participating providers, while the Victoria Project and care providers help review families’ applications. Corporate partnerships also extend to diapers, lactation support and education for growing families.

Welteroth’s own search for care led her to a Black-owned birthing center in Los Angeles. In December 2023, she started a fundraiser to cover care for one family. It brought in enough for two.

The organization formally launched in April 2024, drawing support from individual donors, companies and a network of family funders. That network includes musician John Legend and Chrissy Teigen.

The race organizer lists birthFUND as its official philanthropic partner, with a dedicated fundraising page for supporters of the team.

Their return follows another Houston project. Earlier this month, Rowland and Knowles joined Beyoncé at the opening of the 31-unit Knowles-Rowland House, a permanent supportive housing development. Residents are scheduled to start moving in November 1.

For the walk, participants will travel along Emancipation Avenue, starting near Arbor Street and finishing at Rosalie Street by Emancipation Park. The organizer welcomes children under six with a registered adult, and allows strollers and wheelchairs in the community walk.

The park will host a finishers village with food, music, local businesses and a birthFUND family zone. Registration is open, with the organizer listing a $35 fee. The organizer’s schedule, which is subject to change, places the first race heats at 8 a.m. and the birthFUND community walk at 9:30 a.m. local time on November 28.

item.title: Katt Williams Challenges Hollywood’s Limits On Black Films As He Builds His Own Studio
item.dc:creator: AllHipHop Staff
item.description: Katt Williams explained why he’s building his own studio as he challenged the limits Hollywood places on Black-led movies.
item.content:encoded:
Katt Williams said Black films face tight limits in Hollywood, and he wants his own studio to help change that.

In a new USA TODAY interview, the comic laid out the thinking behind Kemet Movie Works, his film venture in Alabama.

“Nobody needs a complainer, even if they’re correct,” Williams said. “So I can talk blue in the face about what I don’t like about Hollywood.”

He said those complaints should lead him to act once he has a chance to do so. He also said Black films face tighter bounds on the stories they can tell than other films do.

His memoir recounts two times he turned down deals worth millions on principle, USA TODAY reported. He said the business too often loses sight of the people who pay to watch.

The studio effort has a home at Fort McClellan in Anniston, Alabama. Kemet’s site lists film, TV and music work, along with live shows, as part of its plan. That would give creators space to shoot work as well as places to show it.

The venture has been taking shape for some time. Williams credited Tyler Perry’s studio as an example during a 2025 visit to “The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon.”

Kemet’s stated mission is to help a wider range of voices bring film, TV and music projects to life. The firm ties that goal to the region’s Black cultural history, including the Chitlin’ Circuit, a network of venues where Black acts could work during segregation.

Miles College said in May that its deal with Kemet Productions would give students access to AI and augmented-reality film work at the Fort McClellan site. Based in Fairfield, Alabama, Miles is a historically Black college.

He is taking on new work beyond the stage.

Netflix announced in September that he would launch an original podcast on the service later this year. His stand-up shows are already on the service, including “The Last Report.”

His book takes up the question of who controls his work. The publisher says the book explores how he paid for his own tours and kept control of his work. Gallery/13A will release “Nine Lives, No Wives, and 69 Concubines” on October 20.

item.title: Swizz Beatz’s CB2 Deal Started With Alicia Keys’ Nail Tech
item.dc:creator: AllHipHop Staff
item.description: Swizz Beatz traced Casa Dean's start to Dawn Sterling and built his family's DJ roots into a new CB2 furniture collection.
item.content:encoded:
Swizz Beatz credited Alicia Keys’ nail tech with helping him land his CB2 furniture collaboration, then explained how he checked his ego to learn a new craft.

Celebrity manicurist Dawn Sterling connected the producer with someone at the home brand, he revealed in a Wallpaper interview about the collection’s origins.

That introduction led to trips to Chicago to study fabrics and help shape Casa Dean.

“That took being open-minded and not just coming in with the fake celebrity energy. I was more of a student,” Swizz said.

The line brought his family’s name and memories into furniture, lighting and home accessories. Keys also helped him think through the designs. The pair reviewed drawings and photos at their dinner table as the project came together.

One of its most personal pieces was the Lam-Louie DJ console, named for his father. It drew on his grandmother’s cabinet, which had a hidden turntable and record storage. Both Swizz and his dad started as DJs.

Swizz worked with Evan Jerry, founder of Studio ANANSI, during the two-year project. Their goal drew on the home Swizz shares with Keys in La Jolla, California. He wanted pieces the family would actually use in their own space.

His taste had changed since his first home. Back then, Swizz recalled choosing furniture based on price tags and designer names. Travel later helped him form his own views. For Casa Dean, he said he welcomed guidance on colors and materials.

He tied the design work to his day job in a statement on CB2’s collection page.

“The way that I design music is the same part of my brain that I used for designing this collection.”

The Dean family’s creative ties run deep. His uncles Waah and Dee Dean and aunt Chivon Dean co-founded Ruff Ryders, the label and movement that became home to DMX, Eve, The LOX and Swizz himself.

Casa Dean went on sale in stores and online October 15, following early access through the CB2 app a day earlier. The retailer listed the Lam-Louie DJ console at $4,999, with a separate Lam-Louie media console priced at $2,999.

item.title: Method Man Reacts To Wu-Tang’s $4M Album: “I Do Not Hate This Album”
item.dc:creator: AllHipHop Staff
item.description: Method Man praised parts of Wu-Tang’s one-copy album after hearing selections, while holding firm on concerns about its rollout.
item.content:encoded:
Method Man finally heard selections from Wu-Tang Clan’s “Once Upon a Time in Shaolin,” and his first review gave producer Cilvaringz some credit.

“I do not hate this album,” he said on “Pablo Torre Finds Out,” which aired the Brooklyn listening session on October 16. He praised his groupmates and Cilvaringz’s beats, then called the record a “valid piece of art.”

His praise came with limits. He thought some parts ran long and felt Cilvaringz leaned too close to RZA’s sound. He also said he had not sat through the full two-hour record. He wanted a further listen in private.

Method Man still questioned how his work became part of the project. He said he had not known the plan when he recorded his songs and might have contributed more had he understood it.

Those concerns predated the listening party. In 2024, Method Man called the album an uncomfortable subject for Wu-Tang’s members. He said they had been paid to record songs without being told those verses would form a single-copy Wu-Tang release. He viewed the result as a compilation rather than the group album he felt buyers had been promised.

The record’s history helped make it one of rap’s most debated projects. Martin Shkreli bought the sole physical copy in 2015. After his securities-fraud conviction, he forfeited it under a court order. The Justice Department sold the album in July 2021 and applied the proceeds toward his roughly $7.4 million forfeiture judgment.

Pleasr bought the record and said it paid $4 million. The art collective later put parts of the music within fans’ reach. In June 2024, it offered a $1 digital sampler as part of a plan to shorten the wait for a full public release. The original sale terms barred commercial release until 2103.

Netflix began streaming “The Disciple: A Wu-Tang Fable” on October 16. Director Joanna Natasegara traced Cilvaringz’s path from fan to producer, following the recording sessions and art-world ambitions behind a project that kept most listeners outside the room for years. RZA served as an executive producer, and the film marked Natasegara’s feature directing debut.

item.title: A$AP Rocky Says His Kids Still Have Rihanna’s Fame To Discover
item.dc:creator: AllHipHop Staff
item.description: A$AP Rocky reflected on Riot's Copenhagen appearance as his sons began making sense of life with two famous parents.
item.content:encoded:
A$AP Rocky said his children were starting to see their dad perform onstage, but he thought a bigger surprise about Rihanna still awaited them.

The rapper revisited son Riot’s Copenhagen stage appearance in a new Rolling Stone interview. He called the 3-year-old the most outgoing of his siblings and said Riot had asked if his father sang and had also asked A$AP Twelvyy if he made music.

“But I’m like, wait till they get a load of mom, wait till they even realize who their mother is,” he said.

That marked a change from his account in GQ last year. He said RZA and Riot favored children’s songs and did not yet understand their parents’ jobs. They could play his music if they wanted, but had not asked for either parent’s records. He expected questions about his work within a year or two.

The September 18 stop at Copenhagen’s Royal Arena gave Riot a close look at his father’s show. As AllHipHop previously reported, Rihanna brought their son onstage during “Lord Pretty Flacko Jodye 2.” Riot used the megaphone and then shared a fist bump with Rocky.

Rocky’s European run ended in Athens. From Paris, he said the trip had left him a bit homesick.

The boy’s ease in front of a crowd fit a pattern Rocky had described in 2024. He told W that RZA was more reserved, like him, while Riot took after his mother’s outgoing side.

That interview also showed what work had cost him at home. Rocky said he sometimes came back after the boys were asleep and left before they woke. He said fatherhood had changed his schedule and the music that inspired him.

Rihanna had described the same pull between work and family in Harper’s Bazaar last year. She said her sons shaped every choice she made. But doing the work she loved meant time away from them.

She described guilt about showing up for one part of her life while another suffered. She wanted to feel fulfilled when she showed up for her work, and she also wanted to lose the guilt that came with trying to balance it all.

item.title: Snoop Dogg Helps Phonixthecool Build A Catalog He Owns
item.dc:creator: AllHipHop Staff
item.description: Snoop Dogg's mentorship helped Phonixthecool build a catalog he owned while the Durban rapper worked toward Death Row releases.
item.content:encoded:
Snoop Dogg taught Phonixthecool how to earn from music he owned while Death Row Records developed the Durban rapper, the artist said.

In a new Sowetan interview, Phonixthecool described an arrangement that let him release songs on his own while work continued on his Death Row music. He said the goal was to keep an audience and build a catalog that could earn more once the label’s releases drew new listeners.

“Snoop has mentored me on monetising music and using his name while still releasing independently. That way, I own the music,” he said.

The rapper, born Lunga Khumalo, also described the work behind a signing: trying out producers and recording to find the right fit for his voice. He said people often expected a record deal to make an artist a star overnight.

His connection with Snoop reached listeners before the Death Row deal. Phonixthecool appeared with Battle Locco and Kokane on “No Smut On My Name” for 2021’s “Snoop Dogg Presents Algorithm (Global Edition),” released through Def Jam.

Snoop announced the signing in September 2023 while teasing Death Row Africa. By then, the label had become part of his own business, after years in which other companies controlled the name that helped launch his career.

He bought the Death Row brand from MNRK Music Group in February 2022. Funds managed by Blackstone controlled MNRK, and the companies did not disclose the price.

For Snoop, that move began with a desire to regain control of his own recordings. He told TIDAL in 2022 that Jimmy Iovine helped connect him with Blackstone’s David Kestnbaum because Iovine knew he wanted his masters.

“I don’t want to be on nobody’s label. But I’d be on Death Row if I own it. That’s a boss move,” Snoop said then.

He also described a hands-off approach to an artist’s sound. Rather than tell new signees how to rap, he wanted to give artists with a clear musical identity a bigger platform. He said his own experience as a rapper shaped how he handled label business.

Phonixthecool said their contact had mostly been through texts and FaceTime. He planned to visit Los Angeles in January 2027 for his first trip to the United States.

item.title: Nelly & Ashanti Turn Cameras On Her Masters Push & His Touring Grind
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Nelly and Ashanti's new season follows her push to own fresh recordings, his touring toll and their life between two cities.
item.content:encoded:
Nelly and Ashanti’s TV return will follow her push to control her music as he weighs the physical toll of nonstop touring.

Peacock confirmed Thursday that “Nelly and Ashanti: We Belong Together” returns November 19. All eight episodes of the second season will arrive that day, BroadwayWorld reported.

The new season follows Ashanti as she re-records her debut album, works on new music and moves between life in St. Louis and New York City. The season synopsis places that work alongside motherhood, live performances and time with the friends who help keep her grounded.

Nelly’s storyline will explore the physical strain of years on the road.

Ashanti’s ownership project has roots well before the couple’s reality series. She discussed plans to remake her first album during a 2021 appearance on “The Tamron Hall Show”, when she stressed the need to understand record contracts and credited her legal team.

Her self-titled debut, Ashanti, arrived in 2002 and included “Foolish,” “Happy” and “Baby.” The album earned triple-platinum certification.

Ashanti’s stated aim is to own new versions of those songs. Those new performances create separate master recordings from the versions released on her 2002 debut.

“I think it’s really important to stress the importance of ownership. Owning your records, owning your masters,” Ashanti told Rolling Stone AU/NZ in an earlier interview.

She urged artists to understand the business when writing and producing, and said she was re-recording her work. Her remarks put the project in the broader context of artists seeking more control over their creations.

She also singled out “Foolish” as a song that still draws a strong response at shows. Hearing thousands of fans sing words she wrote more than two decades ago remains a highlight of performing, she said.

That same interview offered a glimpse of their offstage chemistry: Ashanti picked Nelly as her favorite collaborator. He joined the video call, joked, “Just making sure,” and kissed her cheek.

The couple’s show was renewed in March 2026 after its June 2025 debut. They began dating in 2003, reunited in 2023 and married that year. The new eight-episode season arrives in full on November 19.

item.title: Lil Wayne Backs Shedeur Sanders Staying In Cleveland After Young Money Deal
item.dc:creator: AllHipHop Staff
item.description: Lil Wayne backed Shedeur Sanders getting his chance in Cleveland after the Browns quarterback hired a Young Money APAA agent.
item.content:encoded:
Lil Wayne backed Shedeur Sanders’ future with the Cleveland Browns after the quarterback hired an agent from the rapper’s Young Money APAA Sports firm.

Asked on “Gridiron” whether he wanted Sanders to leave Cleveland, Wayne made clear he wanted to see the quarterback get his chance where he is. Pro Football Network reported the exchange from his new appearance with Skip Bayless.

“Also, I need him to get his opportunity, and I think where he is, he’s going to get that opportunity,” Wayne said.

The comments carried a business connection beyond Wayne’s interest in football. Sanders hired Young Money APAA CEO Adie von Gontard as his first NFL agent, as AllHipHop reported earlier this week. He went through the draft and the start of his pro career without one.

Wayne did not discuss that hire in his answer. He expressed confidence in Sanders’ future in Cleveland without announcing a move or speaking for the quarterback about his plans.

Cleveland’s current depth chart lists Deshaun Watson first and Sanders second. Head coach Todd Monken chose Watson to open the season after weighing their work through the offseason, training camp, a joint practice and preseason games.

Monken explained in August that the Browns’ opening road games helped shape his choice. He believed Watson gave the team the best chance to run the offense in those settings, including handling the noise and signals away from home.

Since then, Sanders has had little room to show what he can do. Through Cleveland’s first five games, team stats listed one pass, completed for no gain against Carolina. The Browns entered the weekend with a 3-2 record.

Sanders had a larger role as a rookie in 2025. He completed 120 of 212 passes for 1,400 yards, with seven touchdowns and 10 interceptions, before returning to a backup role this season.

Young Money’s ties to Sanders’ former college team already ran through Travis Hunter. The agency represents the Jacksonville Jaguars player, who played alongside Sanders at Colorado. Wayne co-founded the firm with the von Gontard family, and Adie is a certified NFL Players Association agent.

The league’s trade deadline is November 10 at 4 p.m. Eastern.

item.title: RZA Relives Panic Over Wu-Tang’s Martin Shkreli Deal
item.dc:creator: AllHipHop Staff
item.description: RZA accepted Martin Shkreli's place in Wu-Tang history as a new film traced the rare album's troubled path from art to asset.
item.content:encoded:
RZA recalled trying to escape the Martin Shkreli album deal after the buyer’s drug-price scandal, but said a signed contract blocked that exit.

He recounted the panic in a new interview with PEOPLE. Years after the 2015 sale, he accepted Shkreli’s place in Wu-Tang’s story.

“Yes, to be honest. Yes. You got to accept that,” RZA said.

His comments came as “The Disciple: A Wu-Tang Fable” reached streaming. The film follows Cilvaringz, born Tarik Azzougarh, a Dutch-Moroccan rapper who pursued a place within Wu-Tang. His bond with RZA led to the rare album Once Upon a Time in Shaolin.

The 31-track project challenged the idea that recorded music should be cheap and easy to copy. Its creators offered one physical album in a silver box. Shkreli bought it for a reported $2 million in 2015.

RZA, an executive producer and subject of the film, also addressed the work’s future in Netflix’s updated profile. He said he no longer needed to control where it went.

“This has become an entity of its own, and we should allow it to live,” he said.

The album’s path later ran through a federal fraud case. A Brooklyn jury convicted Shkreli in August 2017 of two counts of securities fraud and one count of conspiracy. He cheated investors and rigged a drug company’s stock. A judge sentenced him to seven years in prison.

Shkreli had to give up the record to help pay a roughly $7.4 million judgment. Prosecutors announced its sale on July 27, 2021, saying the money cleared that debt. The case concerned fraud, separate from the drug-pricing scandal RZA recalled.

The concept also caused friction within Wu-Tang. As AllHipHop previously reported, Method Man said in 2024 that members recorded verses without knowing how Cilvaringz would package them. He described the album as a difficult subject within the group.

RZA also said the project had brought him enemies, praise and questions. A small audience could still carry its ideas forward, in his view.

Director Joanna Natasegara said the album challenged how the music business valued art, especially work by artists of color. Her film follows Cilvaringz’s drive to join the group and turn that idea into one rare record. It began streaming October 16.
